title: The Buddhadharma in the World
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Q: “The Buddhadharma is in the world; awakening is not apart from the world.” What does this mean?

inline.s: Q: “The Buddhadharma is in the world; awakening is not apart from the world.” What does this mean?
A: This comes from the “Verses on No-Form” in the *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch*. The full passage is:
“The Buddhadharma is in the world; awakening is not apart from the world. To seek bodhi apart from the world is like seeking a rabbit's horns.”

(Translation: The Buddhadharma is in the world; to awaken, one cannot leave the tempering of the world's dusty conditions. Seeking awakening apart from the tempering of the world's dusty conditions is like seeking rabbit horns, which do not exist.) For the full text of the “Verses on No-Form” and its annotations, see
A Fine Explanation of the Platform Sūtra, Chapter Two: The Prajñā Chapter
“The Buddhadharma is in the world”
— the Buddhadharma is the Way that, in the world, teaches and delivers inverted, deluded living beings so that they may leave the cycle of birth and death.
“Awakening is not apart from the world”

— living beings transmigrate in birth and death precisely because they take the body, thoughts (the shadows of the six sense-objects), and the dusty objects themselves as real, when these are but illusions; thus they pursue objects, create karma, and turn on the wheel of birth and death. Therefore, to leave the cycle of birth and death, one must see through this illusion and cut off all afflictions. This requires testing and tempering oneself in the midst of actual circumstances, examining the mind through every situation. Actual circumstances are the hammer and tongs; apart from the tempering of actual circumstances, one cannot cut off afflictions and leave the three realms, still less realize the Way and attain Buddhahood!

[Shadows of the six sense-objects] When the six sense faculties and the six sense-objects interact, they produce the conditioned mind (thoughts) of delusion, discrimination, and attachment; this conditioned mind is called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantom shadows that appear when the six faculties contact the six objects. On the body, thoughts, and dusty objects being illusions, the Buddha gives a detailed and incisive teaching in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*; see
A Fine Explanation of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment

. [Tempering through actual circumstances] “Tempering” was the ancient method of turning raw iron into steel, as the saying “a hundred temperings make steel” describes. The method: raw iron is repeatedly forged at high temperature to remove impurities, lower the carbon content, and improve its metallurgical structure, until it becomes steel. “Tempering through actual circumstances” means using the grinding and polishing of actual circumstances to remove afflictions and ignorance.
The world refers to the three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The Buddhadharma is the teaching that departs from illusion and realizes truth,
it is a world-transcending Dharma

, and this is the watershed that separates the Buddhadharma from the Confucian way, from outside paths, and from outside paths that masquerade as Buddhism. Nevertheless, the Buddhadharma exists in the world: one must test the mind through actual circumstances in the world in order to break attachments, remove habits, subdue afflictions, cut off afflictions, and leave the world. The Pure Land method needs only to subdue afflictions while reciting the Buddha's name and seeking birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and one can end birth and death and leave the three realms; other methods must cut off afflictions before one can end birth and death and leave the three realms.

[Outside paths masquerading as Buddhism] Sects that attach themselves to Buddhism while distorting and falsifying its teachings. They exploit the human weaknesses of the faithful — fear of difficulty, seeking shortcuts, and craving worldly pleasures — to fool the faithful and swindle fame and gain
“Awakening is not apart from the world”

means that one must work at the very moment of facing circumstances, not flee from them. A practitioner who leaves behind the grinding and polishing of the dusty world is like a flower in a greenhouse: unable to withstand wind and rain, how could he end birth and death? How could he realize the Way and attain Buddhahood?
Master Hanshan Deqing said:

“One who does not forge himself in the midst of circumstances and conditions has only the doings of the gate of light and shadow; when he meets the adverse and favorable states of the eight winds, he will be shaken and carried away, unable to pass through any of them.”
(from the *Dream Roamings
Miscellaneous Sayings at Jingshan*)

[Gate of light and shadow] Refers to seeing the Way not yet truly. The bright moon in the sky is a metaphor for the Way, and the moon's light and shadow in the water is a metaphor for where the Way manifests. One should look up from the light and shadow to gaze at the moon in the sky, and not take the moon's reflection in the water as the true moon. [Eight winds] The “eight winds” are the eight favorable and adverse states of “gain, loss, slander, praise, fame, ridicule, suffering, and joy.” “Gain” is obtaining and advancing; “loss” is declining and retreating; “slander” is being defamed behind one's back, and “praise” is being praised behind one's back; “fame” is being praised to one's face, and “ridicule” is being ridiculed to one's face; “suffering” is all the pain of body and mind, and “joy” is all the pleasure of body and mind. These eight dharmas are what worldly people love and hate, and they can stir up people's hearts, hence they are likened to the “eight winds.”
Q: Why is the Buddhadharma said to be a world-transcending Dharma?

A: The Buddhadharma is to deliver living beings from the three realms and end birth and death, ultimately attaining Buddhahood, and so it is a world-transcending Dharma. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Buddha tells the parable of the burning house:
“There was a great elder, advanced in years, of boundless wealth, with many fields, houses, and servants. His dwelling was vast, with only one door.
Suddenly a fire broke out, burning the house. The elder's children, some ten, twenty, or even thirty, were inside this house.

Within the burning house they delighted in play, unaware and unknowing, without alarm or fear. The fire pressed upon their bodies, pain and suffering upon their very selves; yet their minds felt no loathing and had no thought of seeking escape.

At that time the elder thought: ‘This house is already being consumed by a great fire. If I and my children do not get out in time, we shall surely be burned. Now I must devise an expedient so that the children may escape this harm.’ The father, knowing that the children's hearts each delighted in different things — all manner of rare and wonderful playthings, which they would surely delight in — told them: ‘These playthings you enjoy are rare and hard to obtain; if you do not take them now, you will surely regret it later. Here are all these goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts, now outside the gate, for you to play with. Come out of this burning house quickly! Whatever you wish, I shall give you.’ At that time the children, hearing of these playthings their father described, and because they suited their wishes, each of them grew brave and eager; pushing one another aside, they raced out together, vying to leave the burning house.
At that time the elder gave each of the children one great cart, tall and broad, adorned with all manner of jewels,
drawn by a white ox, pure and clean in hide and body, of fine and beautiful form, with great strength of sinew, walking with even, steady steps, as swift as the wind.
At that time the children, each riding a great cart, obtained what they had never had, and beyond what they had ever hoped for.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is just the same, for he is the father of all the worlds.
But with wisdom and expedient means he rescues living beings from the burning house of the three realms, teaching the three vehicles — of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddha vehicle.
Śāriputra! Just as that elder first enticed his children with three carts, and then gave them only the great cart, adorned with treasures, foremost in safety and peace.”

[Three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world where beings who still have the two desires of lust and food dwell, including the six desire heavens above, humans and animals in the middle, and down to hungry ghosts and hell beings below; the realm of form is the world where beings who are free of the two desires of lust and food but still have a form-body dwell, including the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas; the formless realm is the world where beings who have no form-body but abide with mind and consciousness in profound, subtle meditation dwell, including the four empty heavens (the heaven of boundless space, the heaven of boundless consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception). These three realms are all states of birth-and-death transmigration for ordinary beings, so the first aim of the Buddhist practitioner is to transcend the three realms.

[Burning house] The house is a metaphor for the three realms, and the fire a metaphor for the five defilements and the eight sufferings. Living beings in the three realms are scorched by the five defilements and the eight sufferings, yet do not know how to escape; therefore the Buddha taught the three vehicles (the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle, corresponding to the goat-cart, deer-cart, and ox-cart in the parable) to lure them out of the three realms, and then proclaimed the one Buddha vehicle (the sole teaching of attaining Buddhahood, corresponding to the great white-ox cart in the parable) so that they might ultimately attain Buddhahood.

[Five defilements] 1. The defilement of the age — the era meets with misfortune and disasters arise repeatedly; 2. the defilement of afflictions — people's minds are full of greed, anger, and delusion; 3. the defilement of beings — beings are of inferior quality, with more suffering and less joy; 4. the defilement of views — wrong views spread and thinking becomes confused; 5. the defilement of life-span — beings, repaying evil karma, are worn out in body and mind and their lives are short. [Eight sufferings] 1. The suffering of birth — the pain at the moment of birth; 2. the suffering of aging — the pain of growing old and feeble; 3. the suffering of illness — the pain of being sick; 4. the suffering of death — the pain at the moment of death; 5. the suffering of being separated from what one loves — the pain of parting from those one loves; 6. the suffering of meeting with what one hates — the pain of being with those one hates; 7. the suffering of not getting what one seeks — the pain of one's wishes going unfulfilled; 8. the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates — the pain of the five aggregates (skandhas) blazing intensely and covering over the true nature. [Five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness — the five great elements that constitute body and mind.
Q: In the *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch*, when Prefect Wei asked about rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, why did the Sixth Patriarch answer:

“Ordinary, deluded people do not understand their own nature and do not recognize the Pure Land within their own body, so they wish for the East and wish for the West; for an awakened person, wherever one is, it is the same. Therefore the Buddha said: ‘Wherever one abides, there is constant peace and joy.’”

(Translation: Ordinary, deluded people do not understand their own nature and do not recognize the Pure Land within their own body, so they wish for the East and wish for the West; for an awakened person, wherever one is, it is the same. Therefore the Buddha said: ‘Wherever one abides, there is constant peace and joy.’)

A: These are two different paths of practice: the Pure Land of self-power (the mind-only Pure Land, that is, the “Pure Land within one's own body” mentioned above) and the Pure Land of other-power (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss).
What is called a “Pure Land” is a realm free of the five defilements and the eight sufferings.

The Sixth Patriarch speaks of the Chan path of practice: illumine the mind and see the nature, cut off afflictions, attain the patience of the unborn, and perfectly realize Buddhahood. Its requirement is that in this life one must at least cut off afflictions and leave the three realms. Therefore it pursues the Pure Land of self-power, also called the mind-only Pure Land: when the mind is pure, the land is pure. Hence the Sixth Patriarch says:

“If you constantly practice the ten wholesome deeds, heaven arrives of itself; remove self and other, and Mount Sumeru topples; rid the mind of deviance, and the sea water dries up; without afflictions, the waves are stilled; when poison and harm are removed, the fish and dragons are gone.
The awakened-nature Tathāgata in the ground of your own mind emits great light

, shining outward to purify the six gates and able to break through the heavens of the six desires. When your own nature shines inward, the three poisons are removed, and the offenses of the hells and the rest are destroyed in an instant. Clear and luminous within and without, it is no different from the West. If you do not practice in this way, how can you ever reach it?”
(For annotations, see
A Fine Explanation of the Platform Sūtra
.) This is a practice for those of the very highest faculties; those who can realize the mind-only Pure Land are as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns.

[Patience of the unborn] Abbreviated as the unborn-patience. Realizing that all dharmas are illusions, originally never arisen and therefore without cessation (unborn and unceasing), and abiding unmoving in this principle. “Patience” means abiding — the mind abiding in the principle without wavering. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Forty
the Chapter on Kauṇḍinya, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas are false and unreal.”
The *Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom*
Fascicle Fifty, says:

“The patience of the unborn is to believe, accept, and penetrate the true reality of all dharmas, which are unborn and unceasing, without obstruction and without retreat; this is called the unborn-patience.”

For ordinary people, in this life it is impossible to cut off afflictions and leave the three realms. In that case, a great many people will fall into the evil paths, bobbing up and down in the boundless sea of karma, not knowing in which life they will again be able to practice the Buddhadharma. Therefore the World-Honored One, taking up some soil in his hand, asked Ānanda: “Is there more soil in my hand, or more soil on the great earth?” Ānanda replied: “There is more soil on the great earth.” The Buddha said:
“Those who obtain a human body are like the soil in my hand; those who lose the human body are like the soil of the great earth.”

Hence, “through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, there is no one to lean upon”! Even those who in this life have made considerable progress in ceasing evil and practicing good can hardly escape the “grievance of three lifetimes.”

[Grievance of three lifetimes] Because in this life one ceases evil and practices good, in the next life one enjoys blessed rewards; relying on those blessings, one does evil, which leads to a fall in the life after that. Even if one's hell-karma is exhausted, one is then reborn as a hungry ghost or an animal; to regain a human body is harder than hard!

Therefore, to deliver these living beings who cannot cut off afflictions and leave the three realms in this very life, Amitābha Buddha specially established the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Any living being, as long as at the end of life ten successive recollections of the Buddha are maintained, will be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. (See
The Eighteenth Vow
and
Ten Recollections at the End of Life, Continuous Recollection Brings Rebirth

.) Therefore, every person, as long as the method is correct and the diligence unflagging, can be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and leave the three realms. This is the Pure Land of other-power: being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and leaving the three realms. This is the path on which “ten thousand who practice, ten thousand depart,” the path of practice of the Pure Land school.
